A very sober and hard hitting critique of seasteading from a man who lives on a small island

The article talks a lot about how living on an island like that makes you aware of how deeply dependent every aspect of your life is on the modern supply chain and modern society as a whole, but why couldn't anyone starting a seasteading nation just import the stuff they need or want? Why would that be an issue? Buying a twelve-pack of Coca-Cola isn't going to make you subject to the whims of whatever it is you're trying to get away from. Can't a seastead that wants to separate itself from modern society just slowly wean itself off of those systems so it can learn to make all that crap on its own and not lower its standard of living?

Well sure, of course they can, but it's important to think those supply chains through and work out how they're going to function, which isn't something I see alot of the fancier seasteads doing: Their designs are just appartment blocks on the sea and they expect everything else to just turn up.

I don't see how doing that would be much of a problem though. Couldn't a seastead just trade with a neighboring country or something? They'd need to be recognized by a country that's a part of the UN to be considered their own nation anyway, wouldn't buying stuff from another country help with that?

Trading with another country would not only be desireable, it'd be strictly necessary, but if you're importing literally all your food/consumables and exporting all your waste then life there would be pretty expensive. Plus, doing all of your shopping online would be pretty cumbersome.

It should be taken for granted by anyone forming a seastead that UN recognition isn't going to happen in the next half century at least. If nothing else, floating structures and artificial islands are excluded from the definition of territory.

For an example of what I'm talking about:

http://farm4.static.flickr.com/3301/3497466874_72cf83b534_b.jpg

It's just a box with people in it. I'm not even sure how much storage capacity it has between supply runs.
